title: Samian ware bowl
caption:
This near complete cylindrical bowl is made of terra sigillata, commonly known as Samian ware. Terra sigillata is famous for its red glaze, an effect produced by colouring ordinary glass with red iron oxide, finely ground, and mixed in a thin water slip solution. When fired, the moulded and incised ornaments on the vessels remain visible and distinguishable through the delicate glaze.

This bowl was found at the Roman town of Calleva, near Silchester, during excavations by the Society of Antiquaries in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

Height = 12 cm

Object number REDMG : 1995.81.1

title: Roman penannular brooch
caption:
This penannular brooch was found at the Roman town of Calleva, near Silchester, during excavations by the Society of Antiquaries between 1890 and 1909.

Penannular brooches were common in Roman Britain. They were used to secure clothing. This metal brooch has a hinged pin, which is slightly bent and worn through use.

title: Roman mortarium with food remains
caption:
This pottery mortarium was found at the Roman town of Calleva, near Silchester, during an excavation by the Society of Antiquaries in the late nineteenth century. It probably dates to between 180 and 239 AD and originates from an Oxfordshire kiln. The mortarium would have been used to grind up foods and spices. This one still contains the remains of food pulp comprising varieties of cherry and plum. One of these fruits must have been preserved because they ripen at different times of the year.

Diameter = 22.5 cm

Object number REDMG : 1992.1.1611

title: Beaker with scale decoration
caption:
This partly reconstructed colour-coated ware beaker was made in Gaul, modern day France. The raised scale decoration is barbotine, from the French word for slip, a mixture of clay and water. It probably dates to between 200 and 299 AD. The beaker made its way to Britain and was found at the Roman town of Calleva, near Silchester, during excavations by the Society of Antiquaries in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

title: Roman tile with dog paw prints
caption:
This tile was found at the Roman town of Calleva, near Silchester, during excavations in the 19th and 20th centuries. This tile is impressed with the footprints of two dogs. The prints tell us that tiles were made in the local vicinity and that tiles weren’t wasted, even those spoilt by animals walking across them whilst drying.

title: The Silchester Eagle
caption:
This cast bronze figure of an eagle, known as the Silchester Eagle, was found in the Basilica of the Roman town of Calleva, near Silchester in Hampshire, on the 9th October 1866 during excavations undertaken by Revd J.G. Joyce.

The bird is posed with its wings outstretched, its head raised and turned to the right. The original wings are missing, but it is clear, from the careful modelling of the feathers beneath them, that they must have been extended and raised.

In 1962, Jocelyn Toynbee described the eagle as ‘by far the most superbly naturalistic rendering of any bird or beast as yet yielded by Roman Britain’. It has captured the imaginations of generations of people, including Rosemary Sutcliffe and her novel The Eagle of the Ninth.

Learn more about the Silchester Eagle on the Reading Museum website.

title: The Ogham stone from Silchester
caption:
In 1893, excavators at the Roman town of Silchester (Calleva Atrebatum), Hampshire, discovered a battered small column, about 60cm tall, top-down in a well that had been dug through the foundations of a ruined house. Only when they cleaned it did they realise what they had found. Washing the stone revealed markings which were identified as an ‘inscription written in Ogham characters’. It remains the most easterly find of an Ogham stone to date.

Learn more about this stone on the Reading Museum website, including the meaning of the inscription, the person to whom it was dedicated, and its significance within the wider context of the Roman town of Silchester.

Object number REDMG : 1995.1.24

title: Silchester Baths 2021 Context 3260 buttress
caption: Just beyond the Caldarium, to the East, is this buttress, which may belong to the earlier Neronian bath house. Since this model was created we have excavated further and more walls, contemporary with this structure have emerged. The walls at the east end of the Bath house are built with much deeper foundations because the ground at the east end is very wet due to the Iron Age ditch just a few metres east, and the spring which carried away the run off from the drains of the baths to this ditch.
